persons.name: Mary Barrows
persons.note: INDEPENDENTLY CORROBORATED RESIDENT. Originally documented in Chicago post-office evidence; independent resident research now corroborates the identity. KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, AND HELD THERE MORE THAN ONCE. The papers print 'Barrows, Mary' and 'Mary Barrows' in 2 separate returns of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 28 January 1834, column 1; the Democrat of 20 May 1835, column 13 — across 1834-01-28 to 1835-05-20. A name in a LATER return is somebody still being written to, months on, which is the strongest thing a letter list can say about residence and is why this person outranks a single-return name of the same surname. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1).

persons.name: Chas. H. Chapman
persons.note: INDEPENDENTLY CORROBORATED RESIDENT. Originally documented in Chicago post-office evidence; independent resident research now corroborates the identity. FIRST READ AT THE POST OFFICE, AND THE CORPUS NAMES THEM AGAIN (T-1005). The papers print 'Chas, Ul. Chapman' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 1 April 1834, column 1 — dated 1834-04-01. THE CORPUS NAMES THIS PERSON BESIDE THE RETURN: 3 ordinary readings of the papers, not lists of uncalled-for letters — the Democrat of 26 November 1833 (‘Chapman, C. H.’, chicago_democrat_1833_11_26#c008); the American of 24 December 1833 (‘C. H. Chapman’, chicago_american_1835_06_08#c010); the Democrat of 13 August 1834 (‘Charles H. Chapman’, chicago_democrat_1834_08_13#c012). That is why `letter_list_only` is no longer written on this record: the flag says ‘known only from the post office’ and this record says otherwise. The return below still stands, and is still the weakest thing said here. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Chas. H. Chapman” (f1839_v0198, printed page 42, ward 2, voting for William B. Ogden). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Chapman' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins C. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 4 times, as “CHAPMAN CHARLES H”, 1833-10-22 to 1836-06-28: 1 lot in the platted town — lot 1 of block 4 in the town the register codes CHI (L1BL4CHI, as printed) and 3 parcels of the school section — lot 3 of block 141 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 4 of block 96 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 8 of block 93 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $3149.00 (ls0134, ls0135, ls0136, ls1028). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $2900.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: CHAPMAN CHARLES H matches Chas. H. Chapman: the forename names Chas. H. Chapman of the 2 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

persons.name: Eli B Williams
persons.note: THE 1835 POLL LIST AND A SECOND INDEPENDENT SOURCE. Read from census_1840, directory_1843, directory_1844, newspaper_1833_1835, poll_1834, poll_1835. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1a), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. THE SPRING OF 1833, FROM THE COMPILER'S LIST OF THAT SEASON'S ARRIVALS. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 1 (1895), printed page 90 (claim bk_mose1_005; data/research/books/claims/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.json): "Among the new arrivals in the spring of 1833 are the names of John Dean Caton, John K. Botsford, Silas B. Cobb, Charles Cleaver, Walter Kimball, H. W. Knickerbocker, Ezekiel Morrison, Asahel Pierce, Hibbard Porter, Stephen Rexford, Henry Whitehead, Eli B. Williams, Dr. John T. Temple, Rev. Jeremiah Porter and Rev. Allan B. Freeman." Season precision, carried at 1833-03-01, the first day this project reads a season at (hh_pearsons_hiram, hh_blodgett_tyler_k, hh_kimball_walter, minted off this same list). THE LIST SAYS "AMONG", SO IT IS A ROLL OF EXAMPLES AND NOT A REGISTER: it can date the men it names and it can never be read to exclude anybody it leaves out. THE GRADE CEILING IS THE SOURCE'S AND NOT THIS FIELD'S. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois (1895) is a compiler sixty years after the fact, crediting Andreas and Hurlbut on the pages read here; every claim taken off it is transcription_mediated and none is scan_verified, so nothing drawn from it is graded above `inferred` however plainly it is printed (the rule T-1322 set for the settlers table, kept here). THE POLL'S BOUND IS NOT LOST, IT IS SUBSUMED: a man who came in the spring of 1833 was necessarily in the town for the poll of 1834. The same volume names this man again on page 348 among the eleven who organised the first Episcopal congregation in 1834 (claim bk_mose2_018), which is LATER than this field and therefore bounds nothing — it corroborates a man already here. PRIOR NOTE, KEPT: A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. poll_1834 names this person at Chicago by 31 December 1834 and nothing says when they came. No figure is drawn (L1). OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — A DATE OF DEATH, AND NOTHING ABOUT 1835. John Wentworth's roll of old settlers who had died since 1 January 1881, kept for the Calumet Club and printed in the Chicago Tribune of 25 April 1882, carries “Eli B. Williams, March 24, 1881.”. That corroborates a Chicago residence before 1840 and fixes the END of this life, which this record did not carry; it is not an arrival and it places nobody in the town on 1 July 1835. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Williams, Eli B. | 1833, April, | Tolland, Conn. | 80 | Chicago.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Eli B. Williams,” (f1839_v0050, printed page 41, ward 1, voting for William B. Ogden). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Williams' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins E. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 1 time, as “WILLIAMS ELI B”, 1836-06-21: 1 lot in the platted town — lot 3 of block 16 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L3B16CHIOT, as printed), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $14300.00 (ls1547). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $14300.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: WILLIAMS ELI B matches Eli B Williams: the forename names Eli B Williams of the 3 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE.
